enrichment.short_title: RTA damages for pre-existing cervical degeneration and PTSD
key_facts: The claimant suffered a whiplash injury in a September 1999 head-on collision for which liability was admitted.
He had severe pre-existing cervical degeneration and underwent C6 vertebrectomy; experts disagreed on how soon surgery would otherwise have been needed.
The court found moderately severe PTSD and depression largely attributable to the accident, but rejected much of the claimed loss of earnings as speculative.
General damages were assessed at £35,000 and total damages, after contested heads of loss, were agreed at £1,407,523.16 inclusive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Assessment of damages at trial in the Queen's Bench Division after admitted liability.
enrichment.outcome: Damages assessed in the inclusive sum of £1,407,523.16; defendant ordered to pay the claimant's costs.
enrichment.ratio: A tortfeasor takes his victim as he finds him, but exaggerated or speculative earnings claims may be rejected; where pre-existing degeneration makes surgery likely within about ten years, the claimant remains entitled to compensation for pain, suffering and loss of amenity accelerated by the accident and for genuine psychiatric sequelae.
legal_issues: Acceleration of pre-existing cervical degeneration and extent of lost years
Causation and severity of PTSD and depression
Assessment of future and past loss of earnings for a niche investment consultant
General damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity
index_terms: take your victim as you find him

confidence.notes: Long damages judgment with detailed findings on medical evidence, earnings and final agreed total.

enrichment.short_title: Drink-driving appeal on blood specimen warnings
key_facts: The appellant was convicted after a breath-testing device failed and a blood specimen showed 211 mg alcohol per 100 ml blood.
Justices found he had been warned about prosecution and told he could request part of his blood sample.
On appeal he sought to raise for the first time that the warning must have remained operative in his mind when the sample was taken.
The High Court held that section 2(5) of the 1962 Act had not been re-enacted and no common-law duty to inform of the right to a sample survived.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' conviction, heard out of time with leave.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; order for respondent's costs not to be enforced without leave of the court.
enrichment.ratio: On a case stated appeal a defendant cannot raise a new factual and legal point not put to the justices; absent prejudice and a request to exclude evidence, the absence of a continuing statutory or common-law obligation to inform a motorist of the right to a split blood sample does not require acquittal.
legal_issues: Whether new issues may be raised on appeal by case stated
Whether motorists must be told of the right to request part of a blood specimen under section 7 RTA 1988
Effect of R v Price and R v Mitten under the 1962 and 1988 road traffic legislation
Admissibility of blood analysis where no prejudice is shown
linked_authorities: DPP v Jackson and Stanley v DPP

confidence.notes: Short, focused judgment with clear statutory analysis and defined outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Confiscation after father's repayment of benefit fraud
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to long-running council tax and social security frauds and received concurrent 22-month sentences.
A confiscation order of £118,660.69 was made, including £38,000 representing increased equity in the family home.
Before sentencing his father paid £81,819.24 to reimburse the unlawfully obtained benefits.
The sentencing judge had already taken the repayment into account and made no compensation order because restitution had been made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against part of a confiscation order under the unamended Criminal Justice Act 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Confiscation order reduced to £78,000; appeal allowed in part.
enrichment.ratio: Under the general discretion in section 71(1) of the unamended Criminal Justice Act 1988, a court may take account of repayment of benefits to victims, but repayment by a relative rather than the offender himself warrants only partial credit because the offender may still enjoy the use of equivalent assets pending repayment of the familial debt.
legal_issues: Exercise of discretion under section 71(1) of the unamended 1988 Act
Effect of a third-party repayment of fraud proceeds before confiscation
Relationship between confiscation and compensation orders
Application of authorities including Brazil, Layode, Williams, Mitchell and Smith

confidence.notes: Detailed Court of Appeal analysis of confiscation discretion with a precise substituted figure.

enrichment.short_title: Hedley Byrne duty in asbestos reinsurance broking dispute
key_facts: EIR sought to avoid a 1996 asbestos reinsurance contract with Curzon for alleged non-disclosure of a Mendes & Mount market report.
Curzon brought Part 20 claims against Sedgwick group companies and employees for negligent broking and assumed responsibility in placing reinsurance.
SRS, SOL and Marsh applied to set aside their joinder or strike out the Part 20 claim as having no real prospect of success.
The letter of engagement between T&N and SL limited SL's contractual liability, but Curzon was not a party to that contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside joinder or strike out Part 20 claims in commercial proceedings after a case management conference order joining defendants without merits determination.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; joinder of SRS, SOL and Marsh to stand and Part 20 claims to proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: A Hedley Byrne assumption-of-responsibility claim against insurance brokers and their employees is not bound to fail at a summary stage merely because a related contractual engagement limited another group's liability to T&N; Curzon's separate exposure and the pleaded involvement of individual brokers give the claim a real prospect of success.
legal_issues: Test for striking out or setting aside Part 20 joinder
Whether SRS, SOL and Marsh assumed responsibility to Curzon in tort
Effect of the T&N letter of engagement and contractual limitation clauses
Vicarious and personal Hedley Byrne liability of employees Hammond and Herrick
linked_authorities: Three Rivers DC v Bank of England
Standard Chartered Bank v Pakistan Shipping Corpn

confidence.notes: Substantive procedural judgment applying settled Hedley Byrne principles to detailed pleaded facts.

enrichment.short_title: Flying Squad officers' appeal over stolen robbery proceeds
key_facts: Three Metropolitan Police Flying Squad officers were convicted of conspiring to steal and perverting justice over the guard's £200,000 share of a £1.5m Security Express robbery in January 1995.
The Crown case relied heavily on corrupt officer Kevin Garner and informant Hector Harvey, supported by circumstantial financial evidence.
Each appellant received five years on the conspiracy count and seven years concurrent on the perversion count.
The appeal raised abuse of process, exclusion of Garner's evidence, jury directions, disclosure and PII issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Full Court of Appeal criminal appeal after renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction and sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Convictions upheld as safe; applications for leave to appeal against sentence refused.
enrichment.ratio: Convictions based on the combined evidence of accomplices and supporting circumstantial material may remain safe where trial judges properly exercised discretion on abuse of process and section 78 exclusion, and where alleged defects in summing up or disclosure did not render the verdicts unsafe.
legal_issues: Admissibility and fairness of accomplice evidence from Garner
Abuse of process arising from police inducements to Garner
Adequacy of disclosure and public interest immunity handling
Safety of convictions for conspiracy to steal and perverting the course of justice
Appropriateness of seven-year concurrent sentences

confidence.notes: Very long judgment; core outcome and central issues are explicit though many subsidiary grounds were rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Maintenance judgment summons after remarriage loans
key_facts: A 1997 consent order required the husband to pay £22,000 per annum periodical payments until remarriage or further order.
After remarriage in 2001 he reduced payments while borrowing about £41,000 from his new wife and prioritised repaying her from sale proceeds of his flat.
A judgment summons for £11,297 arrears was heard before Mr Justice Hedley, who imposed one month's imprisonment suspended on payment.
The process used Form N17 and did not follow the Article 6-compliant procedure later reflected in Mubarak and the 2003 rule amendments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against committal order made on a judgment summons under the Debtors Act 1869.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; committal order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: A judgment summons process that fails to comply with Mubarak and Convention standards, reverses the burden of proof and proceeds before variation of periodical payments is determined cannot support committal; the payer's obligation to his new wife does not without more establish wilful neglect of the earlier maintenance order.
legal_issues: Human Rights Act compliance of judgment summons procedure
Burden and standard of proof for wilful neglect under the Debtors Act 1869
Use of Family Proceedings Rules 7.4(9) to vary or suspend periodical payments
Whether arrears were absolute before a variation application
Relationship between judgment summons and variation proceedings

confidence.notes: Clear Court of Appeal procedural ruling with detailed discussion of Mubarak and the 2003 rule reforms.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum delay and Article 8 family reunion damages claim
key_facts: An Angolan refugee was eventually granted asylum in August 2001 after a successful Court of Appeal remittal to the IAT.
His family obtained entry clearance in November 2002; he claimed unlawful delay in granting status and impeding family reunion applications.
The court found about six months' unreasonable delay in issuing the formal status letter after the IAT determination but no Article 8 breach.
Had Article 8 been breached, the judge indicated damages of about £1,000 to £2,000 rather than £12,000 sought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review and Human Rights Act claim for damages; permission refused on renewed application after refusal on the papers.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal granted to the claimant and to the Secretary of State on specified issues.
enrichment.ratio: Unreasonable delay in implementing a successful asylum appeal may breach domestic public law duties without necessarily interfering with Article 8 family life where reunion was ultimately achieved and systemic immigration delay was not shown to lack effective respect for family life.
legal_issues: Whether delay in granting refugee status breached Article 8
Availability of damages under section 8 Human Rights Act 1998
Unlawfulness of delay after IAT determination
Effect of delay on family entry clearance applications
Quantum of non-pecuniary damages for family separation
linked_authorities: Anufrijeva v Mayor & Burgesses of London Borough of Southwark

confidence.notes: Long judgment with mixed findings; primary Article 8 outcome and permission order are clear.

enrichment.short_title: NASS dispersal and local connection under Housing Act 1996
key_facts: Two former asylum seekers housed under NASS in Glasgow later became eligible for homelessness assistance in London boroughs.
Each authority sought to refer the case to Glasgow City Council on the basis of local connection through past residence.
NASS accommodation is allocated on a no-choice basis and section 97(2)(a) forbids regard to the supported person's locality preference.
The Court of Appeal held by a 2-1 majority that such residence is not residence of the applicant's own choice for section 199(1)(a).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals to the Court of Appeal on points of law from county court decisions under section 204 Housing Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; county court decisions upholding referral to Glasgow set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Where asylum support legislation requires a provider to ignore any preference as to locality, residence in NASS-dispersed accommodation cannot be treated as normal residence of the occupant's own choice for the purpose of establishing a local connection under section 199(1)(a) of the Housing Act 1996.
legal_issues: Whether NASS accommodation can create local connection under section 199(1)(a)
Meaning of normal residence of the applicant's own choice
Interaction between the Housing Act 1996 and Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 dispersal scheme
Application of Mohamed v Hammersmith and Fulham LBC
Referral of homeless applicants between local housing authorities
linked_authorities: Mohamed v London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham
R v Barnet LBC ex parte Shah
R v Eastleigh Borough Council ex parte Betts

confidence.notes: Leading split Court of Appeal decision with clearly stated ratio from the majority.

enrichment.short_title: High-security patient challenge to MHRT transfer recommendation
key_facts: Patient P is detained at Ashworth Hospital under restriction orders following 1972 index offences of manslaughter and rape.
A Mental Health Review Tribunal in July 2002 recommended trial leave in medium security at Chadwick Lodge but the move was not implemented.
The Responsible Medical Officer and Secretary of State opposed transfer, citing high risk and need for sex offender treatment.
P sought judicial review and a section 7 Human Rights Act claim alleging Article 8 required implementation of the Tribunal recommendation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review and Human Rights Act claim after refusal on the papers.
enrichment.outcome: Permission for judicial review refused; section 7 claim withdrawn contingent on that refusal.
enrichment.ratio: Article 8 does not transform an extra-statutory MHRT recommendation into a binding direction; decisions on leave, transfer and consent under the Mental Health Act 1983 remain for the RMO and Secretary of State, who must take the recommendation into account but are not bound by it.
legal_issues: Legal effect of MHRT recommendations on transfer from special hospital
Powers under sections 17, 19 and 123 Mental Health Act 1983
Whether Article 8 requires implementation of recommended medium-security trial leave
Role of the court versus statutory decision-makers in assessing risk
Relationship between judicial review and section 7 Human Rights Act claims
linked_authorities: R v Home Secretary ex parte Harry
R (Home Secretary) v Mental Health Review Tribunal
R (Wilkinson) v Broadmoor Special Hospital Authority
R (Brandenberg) v East London and City NHS Trust

confidence.notes: Permission judgment with clear legal framework and explicit refusal of permission.

enrichment.short_title: Excise forfeiture proportionality for cross-border shopping
key_facts: Customs seized excise goods and an Austin Montego car after a random stop at the Channel crossing in April 2001.
Mrs Reed had bought tobacco and cigarettes with money from her daughter and son-in-law who did not travel; other passengers' goods were for their own use.
Magistrates condemned the goods as forfeit; the Crown Court allowed Mr Newbury's appeal on proportionality and seizure lawfulness grounds.

The Court of Appeal held Mrs Reed's goods were liable to forfeiture but Mr Newbury's goods and Mrs Newbury's car were not, and courts may refuse condemnation where forfeiture would breach Convention or EU rights.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Crown Court to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed in relation to Mr Newbury's goods and Mrs Newbury's car; question 2 answered yes and question 3 confirms court jurisdiction to refuse disproportionate condemnation.
enrichment.ratio: Goods imported for another person's reimbursed purchase are not the traveller's own-use imports protected by Article 8 of Directive 92/12; mixed goods and a vehicle used to carry them are not liable to forfeiture where condemnation would be a disproportionate interference with EU free-movement rights or Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR rights of innocent owners.
legal_issues: Whether reimbursed cross-border purchases are own-use imports under Directive 92/12
Liability to forfeiture of mixed goods and vehicles under sections 49 and 141 CEMA
Court's jurisdiction to refuse condemnation on proportionality grounds after Hoverspeed
Interaction of condemnation proceedings with Human Rights Act and EU law
Application of Lindsay v Customs and Excise Commissioners
linked_authorities: Lindsay v Customs and Excise Commissioners
R (Hoverspeed) v Commissioners of Customs and Excise
Conegate Ltd v HM Customs and Excise
Gascoyne v Customs and Excise Commissioners

confidence.notes: Court of Appeal judgment with stated questions answered explicitly and detailed EU/HRA analysis.
